problem: Outdoor mapless urban navigation needs perception that covers an open set of factors (terrains, semantics, dynamic entities) and costs aligned with operator preferences. Prior methods rely on hand-enumerated classes, large robot datasets for imitation, or hand-tuned multi-term rewards, and zero-shot VLMs are poorly attuned to navigation.
motivation: Enumerating every relevant navigation factor is infeasible and large expert datasets are costly. Visual foundation models carry robust open-set priors, and human operators can cheaply say which paths are bad. The paper combines VFM distillation with counterfactual feedback to learn robust BEV features and expert-aligned rewards from only 3 hours of data.
key_idea: Distill DINOv2 features and SAM2 instance structure into a lightweight image-to-BEV encoder, then learn a BEV reward map with a counterfactual IRL objective that pushes reward down on operator-flagged bad paths and up on expert paths, via an active learning loop.
insight: Both components matter: removing counterfactuals (-cfs) raises interventions about 3x (70% fewer with counterfactuals in seen, 69% in unseen), and removing the structured BEV backbone (-st) adds 28% more interventions (41% without both). Only 1-5 negative counterfactual annotations on 3% of the data significantly help reward learning. Distilled DINOv2 features beat frozen DINOv2, and LiDAR depth adds robustness to lens flare over RGB-only or stereo. The GPT-4o-mini-based PIVOT baseline performs poorly, suggesting VLMs are poorly attuned to fine-grained urban navigation.
method: Perceptual encoder Θ (25.5M): TerrainNet-style EfficientNet-B0 RGB-D encoder with a depth-completion head (binned cross-entropy), lift-splat to BEV, and a U-Net/ResNet18 BEV inpainting backbone with separate decoders.

DINOv2 distillation: the semantic decoder regresses frozen DINOv2 image features (MSE) from the latent RGB-D features, so the encoder inherits open-set semantics and robustness to lighting and viewpoint.

SAM2 instance-aware BEV heads: static and dynamic panoptic decoders trained with supervised contrastive loss on BEV instance maps, plus an L1 elevation head. Labels are auto-generated from SAM2 masks, LiDAR backprojection, DBSCAN clustering, IoU-based cross-frame merging and pose accumulation, giving a structured BEV map of static, dynamic and elevation channels.
Reward function r_φ: a 0.5M multi-scale FCN mapping the BEV features to a scalar reward map, trained with a Value Iteration Network policy over an 8-connected grid.

Counterfactual IRL loss: min_π max_φ E_ρE[r] − (α E_ρS[r] + (1−α) E_ρπ[r]), derived from Bradley-Terry ranking. It reduces to apprenticeship learning at α=0 and to preference learning at α=1, with reward regularization.

Active counterfactual loop: warmstart with expert data only, then flag samples with large Hausdorff distance between policy rollout and expert. Generate about 10 alternate paths by perturbing 3 control points with Gaussian offsets (μ=±1, σ=0.5) and Hybrid A*. A human marks bad paths as counterfactuals and r_φ is retrained with α=0.5.

Navigation stack: OpenStreetMap coarse GPS subgoals every 10 m, a carrot at the edge of a 6 m local horizon, DWA-style scoring of 31 constant-curvature arcs on the inverted reward costmap plus a goal-reaching cost weighted 1/10, and 1D time-optimal control.

setting.backbone: EfficientNet-B0 RGB-D encoder + ResNet18 BEV backbone (25.5M) + 0.5M MS-FCN reward net, with DINOv2 and SAM2 used as teachers/label generators (trained)
setting.training_data: 3 hours of self-collected expert robot demonstrations (parks, downtown, residential, campus; synchronized image-LiDAR with LeGO-LOAM poses), 3% annotated with negative counterfactuals; DINOv2/SAM2 pseudo-labels; 150 epochs total
setting.observation: monocular RGB (512x612, 110° FOV) + sparse depth from 128-channel LiDAR, coarse phone GPS + magnetometer
setting.action_space: 31 constant-curvature arcs (DWA-style) scored on a BEV reward map, executed with 1D time-optimal control
setting.privileged: none (OpenStreetMap coarse waypoints; a geometric obstacle-avoidance module is used for all methods)

numbers_note: Real-world robot experiments only; no standard benchmarks. Metrics are AST (s, lower better), %S, and NIR (interventions per 100 m, lower better). Short-horizon results are from only 2 repeats per location (5 for Blanton).
results: CREStE beats all baselines (Geometric-Only, PACER+G, ViNT, PIVOT) in every short-horizon location, seen and unseen. The strongest baseline, PACER+G, needs 2x more interventions in seen and 5x more in unseen areas, and CREStE is intervention-free in Woolridge Square and Hemphill Park. On a 1.9 km unseen trail CREStE needs 1 intervention (NIR 0.052, 99.45% subgoals) versus 48 for PACER+G (NIR 3.56, 61.53%), which timed out after 1345 m.
limitations: Reward maps come from a single timestep, with no memory, so dead ends and constricted spaces are hard, and rewards are not conditioned on embodiment.
Counterfactual labeling still needs a human annotator (about 2 h for the dataset), and the results are on one robot (Jackal) with few trials per location.
Baselines (PACER, PIVOT) are reproductions without official code and all share a geometric avoidance module, so comparisons are hard to replicate.
